shares.title: Shared folders
shares.intro: Every shared folder is its own dataset on a pool, with its own space and restore points. Choose who may read or change its files.
shares.caption: Shared folders with their pool, space, description and rights
shares.empty: No shared folders yet. Create one to store files together.
shares.rights: {count, plural, =0 {Administrators only} one {# user} other {# users}}

createDialog.title: Create a shared folder
createDialog.name: Name
createDialog.nameHint: Letters, digits, spaces, dots, dashes and underscores.
createDialog.noPools: No pool is ready for shared folders yet. Create a pool in Storage first.
createDialog.dataset: The shared folder becomes the dataset {dataset}.

editDialog.title: Edit {name}
editDialog.name: Name
editDialog.datasetKept: Renaming changes only the name users see; the dataset keeps its name.
editDialog.rightsIntro: Changes apply right away. A user gets the most that it or one of its groups is given; administrators can always read and change everything.
editDialog.protocolsIntro: Users reach this folder over the protocols allowed for them on the Users page.
editDialog.smbEncryptHint: Older clients without SMB encryption cannot connect then.

deleteDialog.title: Delete {name}
deleteDialog.keepDataset: The shared folder goes away. The dataset {dataset} and its files stay and remain in Storage.
deleteDialog.keepFolder: The shared folder goes away. The files stay in the folder {path}.
deleteDialog.destroyHint: The dataset, all its files and every snapshot are deleted. This cannot be undone.
deleteDialog.folderOnly: This is a plain folder, not a dataset, so its files can only be kept.
deleteDialog.nothingRuns: No command runs. {location} and its files stay.

fileServices.intro: File services let other computers open your shared folders over the network. Users sign in with their Pithyx user name and password.

firewall.title: Firewall
firewall.explain: Pithyx lets other computers reach only the web interface and the file services that are switched on. Switching a service off also closes its port.
firewall.privateSwitch: Only private networks may use the file services
firewall.privateExplain: SMB, SFTP, SSH and FTP then answer only computers in private networks (10.x, 172.16 to 31.x, 192.168.x, link-local and IPv6 ULA). Leave it off if you reach the box through a router from another network or over a VPN with public addresses. The web interface stays reachable either way.
firewall.inactive: This is a development machine: Pithyx keeps the rules but does not apply them here.

fileServices.rights: Who may use which file service is set with the rights of each user or group on the Users and Groups pages. Which shared folders they offer is set per folder on the Shared folders page. A user who has not signed in on the web since file services arrived must sign in once, so the services learn the password.

smb.title: SMB
smb.explain: Network drives for Windows, macOS and Linux. Only encrypted, signed connections of current systems (SMB 3) are accepted.
smb.workgroupHint: Up to 15 letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores. Most networks use WORKGROUP.
smb.mac: macOS and Linux: connect to the server
smb.trash: Files deleted over SMB go to the shared folder's recycle bin, where Files can restore them.
smb.versions: Restore points show as "Previous versions" in Windows.

sftp.title: SFTP
sftp.explain: Encrypted file transfer over SSH, for example with FileZilla, WinSCP or the sftp command. Users see only their shared folders and get no shell.
sftp.view: Switching SFTP off only stops letting Pithyx users in; it does not stop SSH for other accounts.

ssh.title: SSH logins
ssh.explain: Users with the right to sign in over SSH get a shell on the box. Off by default.
ssh.switch: Let users with the SSH login right sign in with a shell
ssh.warning: A shell reaches the whole system with the user's rights. Give the right only to people who need it. Switching this off never stops SSH for the system's own accounts.

webdav.title: WebDAV
webdav.explain: Shared folders as a network drive over the web address of the box, for example in a file manager or a sync program. Users sign in with their Pithyx user name and password. Off by default.
webdav.trash: Files deleted over WebDAV go to the shared folder's recycle bin, and new files belong to the user who wrote them.

ftp.title: FTP
ftp.explain: For devices and programs that know neither SFTP nor WebDAV, such as scanners. Encrypted connections (FTP with TLS, also called FTPS), plain FTP only if you allow it below, and only passive mode. Off by default.
ftp.switch: Offer shared folders over FTP with TLS
ftp.plainSwitch: Also allow plain FTP without encryption
ftp.plainWarning: At your own risk: without encryption, user names, passwords and files cross the network readable for anybody on it. Allow it only for devices that cannot use TLS, and only on a network you trust. Refusing it again ends every unencrypted session.
ftp.tls: Choose "explicit FTP over TLS" in your program. The box has its own certificate, so the program asks once whether to trust it; compare the fingerprint below.

network.intro: How this box is connected: its network cards, bonds and VLANs. Every change waits 60 seconds for your confirmation and goes back on its own without it, so a wrong address cannot lock you out.
network.notChangeable: Pithyx does not change this interface on this machine.

bondModeHints.activeBackup: One card carries the traffic; another takes over when its cable fails. Works with every switch.
bondModeHints.lacp: All cards together. The switch ports must form an LACP group.
bondModeHints.balanceAlb: All cards send and receive without help from the switch.

draft.label: Changes not applied yet
draft.text: You changed the network settings. Nothing is applied until you press Apply; all changes then apply together.
draft.waiting: Keep or undo the waiting change first.

pending.label: Network change waiting for confirmation
pending.title: {seconds, plural, one {# second} other {# seconds}} left to keep the new network settings
pending.text: The new settings are active. Keep them, or the box goes back to the previous ones on its own.
pending.fromConsole: Someone at the box's console changed the network. Keep the change here or on the console, or the box goes back on its own.
pending.openNew: If this page stops answering, open the box at its new address and keep the change there:

global.title: Host name and name servers
global.hostNameHint: Letters, digits and hyphens. Windows networks see its first 15 characters.
global.dnsHint: Up to four addresses, separated by spaces. Empty uses those DHCP announces; set ones replace them.
global.searchDomainsHint: Tried for short names, separated by spaces.
global.defaultRouteHint: When several interfaces have a gateway, this one carries the traffic to other networks.
global.notChangeable: Pithyx does not change the host name and name servers of a development machine.

dialog.name: Name
dialog.nameHint: Up to 15 lower-case letters, digits, dots and hyphens.
dialog.noCards: No free network card. A card with its own settings must go back to DHCP first.
dialog.vlanIdHint: 1 to 4094, as the switch port tags it.
dialog.mtuHint: Empty keeps the default (1500). Jumbo frames need every device on the way to agree, up to 9000.
dialog.connectionWarning: This browser reaches the box through this interface. A mistake here interrupts the connection until the change goes back after 60 seconds.

apply.title: Apply network settings
apply.text: The new settings apply at once. You then have {seconds} seconds to keep them; otherwise the box goes back to the previous settings on its own.
apply.connectionWarning: This browser reaches the box through {name}, which changes. The page may stop answering; open the new address or wait 60 seconds for the old settings to come back.
apply.addresses: The box will also answer at:

certificates.intro: The box speaks HTTPS on port 7484; ports 80 and 443 send every visitor there, unless a host of the reverse proxy has the name. It is its own certificate authority: install its root once on a device, and the device trusts the box and every certificate the box issues.

connection.title: Connection
connection.explain: The web interface and FTPS present this certificate. A browser warns about it until the device trusts the box's root.
connection.plain: This daemon serves plain HTTP: it runs for development or simulation. A box always uses HTTPS.

trust.title: Trust this box
trust.explain: Download the root certificate and install it on every device that uses the box. Afterwards the browser shows no warning, reloads come from its cache and FTPS clients accept the box.
trust.compare: Before you trust the file on a device, compare its fingerprint with the one above.

windows.name: Windows:
windows.steps: Open the file, choose Install Certificate, Local Machine, then the store Trusted Root Certification Authorities.

macos.name: macOS:
macos.steps: Open the file in Keychain Access (keychain System), open the certificate and set Trust to Always Trust.

ios.name: iPhone and iPad:
ios.steps: Open the file in Safari and install the profile under Settings, General, VPN and Device Management, then switch it on under Settings, General, About, Certificate Trust Settings.

android.name: Android:
android.steps: Settings, Security, Encryption and credentials, Install a certificate, CA certificate, then pick the file.

linux.name: Linux:
linux.steps: Copy the file to /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/ and run sudo update-ca-certificates; browsers with their own store need the step below.

firefox.name: Firefox:
firefox.steps: Settings, Privacy and Security, Certificates, View Certificates, Authorities, Import, and trust it to identify websites.

authority.title: Certificate authority
authority.explain: A root, which devices trust, and an intermediate, which signs every certificate. The intermediate renews itself a year before it ends, without devices noticing.
authority.unrestricted: This authority may sign any name. A device that trusts it would also accept a forged certificate for any website if someone took over the box.

dialog.title: Create a new certificate authority?
dialog.explain: Every device has to trust the new root again. Certificates issued for other devices stay valid only where the old root is still trusted.
dialog.restricted: Only local names and private addresses (recommended)
dialog.suggested: Always included: {domains}, and the private address ranges.
dialog.domainsHint: Optional, separated by spaces or commas, such as home.example.org. Each covers every name below it.
dialog.unrestrictedWarning: Without the limit, a device that trusts the box accepts any certificate it signs, also for banks and other websites. Choose this only if you need it and keep the box secure.

names.title: Names of the box's certificate
names.explain: The box's certificate covers its host name, its addresses and these names, and is issued again when one of them changes.
names.extraHint: For example a domain that points at the box, separated by spaces or commas. It has to lie inside what the authority may sign.

issued.title: Certificates for other devices
issued.explain: Issue certificates for printers, routers or other servers in your network. Every device that trusts the box's root trusts them too.

issueDialog.title: Issue a certificate
issueDialog.explain: The certificate and its private key are downloaded as two files. The box does not keep the key, so store it safely.
issueDialog.namesHint: Separated by spaces or commas, such as printer.lan 192.168.1.30. *.media.lan covers every name below media.lan.
issueDialog.daysHint: 1 to 825 days. Apple devices refuse longer validities.
issueDialog.rsa: RSA key for devices that do not support ECDSA
issueDialog.done: Done. Check your downloads for the .crt and .key files.

removeDialog.title: Remove the certificate for {names}?
removeDialog.explain: It only leaves this list. The box keeps no revocation list, so the certificate stays valid until it ends.

custom.title: Your own certificate
custom.explain: Instead of the box's own certificate, present one you got elsewhere, for example for your own domain. The box uses it while it is valid and then goes back to its own.
custom.unused: This certificate is not valid now, so the box presents its own.

proxy.intro: Make other services reachable under their own names on ports 443 and 80: the box forwards each name to its target and presents a certificate for it. The box itself stays on port 7484; names nobody set up go there as before.

options.title: Ports and unknown names
options.ports: Proxy hosts answer HTTPS on port {tls} and plain HTTP on port {plain}.
options.plainOnly: Proxy hosts answer plain HTTP on port {plain}; this daemon has no HTTPS.
options.noPorts: This daemon does not listen on ports 443 and 80 (development or simulation). You can set up hosts, but they only answer on a box.
options.unknownRedirect: Redirect to the web interface on port 7484
options.signInAddressHint: Where hosts with the Pithyx sign-in send visitors, such as https://nas.home.arpa:7484. Leave it empty to use the requested name on port 7484.

hosts.title: Proxy hosts
hosts.explain: A proxy host forwards requests for its domains to a service in your network or on this box. Point the domains at the box in your DNS or router.
hosts.log: Access log in the Log Center under {source}

redirects.title: Redirect hosts
redirects.explain: A redirect host sends browsers from its domains to another address, for example from an old name to a new one.

streams.title: Streams
streams.explain: A stream forwards a TCP or UDP port of the box byte for byte to another host, for services that do not speak HTTP. The firewall opens the port.

remove.hostExplain: Its names are unknown afterwards. An uploaded certificate is deleted with it.
remove.streamExplain: The box stops forwarding and the firewall closes the port.

certificate.label: Certificate
certificate.boxHint: The box makes a certificate for the domains. They must lie in its authority's scope (Settings > Certificates); devices that trust the box's root accept it.
certificate.customHint: A certificate with its chain and unencrypted private key in PEM that covers every domain, for example for a public domain.
certificate.stored: A certificate is uploaded. Choose new files only to replace it.

tls.systemHint: For targets with a certificate from a public authority.
tls.boxHint: For devices with a certificate the box issued.
tls.noneHint: For targets with a self-signed certificate. The connection is encrypted, but anyone in between could pose as the target.

fields.domainsHint: Separated by commas or spaces, for example media.home.arpa or *.apps.home.arpa (a wildcard covers one level).
fields.targetHostHint: A host name or IP address in your network.
fields.onBox: The target is a service on this box itself
fields.hstsWarning: With HSTS browsers refuse plain HTTP and every certificate warning for this name for a year, even after you switch it off. Use it only with a certificate all devices trust.
fields.allowHint: IP addresses or ranges such as 192.168.1.0/24, separated by commas. Empty lets everybody in.
fields.signInExplain: Visitors sign in with their account on the box first. Signing out of the box ends their access. The target gets the user in X-Pithyx-User and X-Pithyx-Groups.
fields.usersHint: Names separated by commas. With no users and no groups, everybody who may sign in gets in; administrators always do.
fields.basicAuthHint: Asks the browser for a name and password before anything else, also for apps without a sign-in of their own.
fields.basicPasswordKeep: Leave it empty to keep the password.
fields.preserveHost: Send the requested name as Host
fields.hostHeaderHint: Optional. Sends this Host to the target instead.
fields.headersHint: One per line as Name: value. Name: alone removes the header.
fields.redirectTargetHint: A complete address such as https://new.example.org.
fields.portHint: Not one of the box's own ports (21, 22, 80, 443, 445, 7484, 50000 to 50099).

regional.intro: Language, formats and time of the box. Everyone can still choose their own language in the user menu.
regional.languageHint: The sign-in page uses it, and so does everyone whose browser asks for a language Pithyx does not have.
regional.formatsHint: How dates, times and numbers look for everyone, for example 31.12.2026 or 12/31/2026.
regional.serversHint: Host names or addresses, separated by spaces. Leave empty for the default servers.

restorePoints.title: What are restore points?
restorePoints.what: Once a day, Pithyx keeps the state of a shared folder as a restore point and keeps each one for 7 days. New shared folders have them switched on.
restorePoints.restore: Deleted or overwritten a file by mistake? Right-click it in Files and choose “Previous versions” to get an earlier state back.
restorePoints.space: A restore point takes space only for files that were changed or deleted after it. Example: in a folder with 100 GB of photos you edit 1 GB of them; the restore points then need about 1 GB more, not another 100 GB.
restorePoints.deleted: A deleted file frees its space only when the last restore point that still holds it expires. Example: you delete a 4 GB video; it is gone from the folder at once, but its 4 GB come free after 7 days.
restorePoints.protects: They help against accidental deletes and against ransomware: a folder that malware encrypted can be brought back to the state before.
restorePoints.notBackup: Restore points live on the same disks as your files. They are no replacement for a backup on another device.

backup.intro: A configuration backup holds everything needed to set this box up again: users, groups and passwords, shared folders and their rights, file services, storage schedules, regional settings, certificates and SSH keys. It does not hold the files on your pools.

create.title: Create a backup
create.intro: The backup is downloaded as one file, encrypted with a password you choose. Keep it somewhere other than this box.
create.keepPassword: Without this password the backup cannot be restored. Pithyx does not keep it, and nobody can recover it.

restore.title: Restore a backup
restore.intro: Choose a backup file and enter its password. Pithyx checks the file first; nothing changes until you confirm.
restore.counts: {users, plural, one {# user} other {# users}}, {groups, plural, one {# group} other {# groups}}, {sharedFolders, plural, one {# shared folder} other {# shared folders}}
restore.warning: Each part you choose replaces the current one completely. Files on your pools stay untouched. Pithyx restarts afterwards.
restore.restarting: The configuration was restored. Pithyx restarts and this page loads again in a moment.
restore.problems: Some steps did not work; the Log Center has the details:

confirm.title: Restore the configuration?
confirm.body: These parts are replaced by the backup:
confirm.signOut: Restoring the users signs everybody out, you included. Sign in again with an account and password from the backup.

users.title: Users and groups
users.description: Accounts, groups, passwords (also for SMB and SFTP), two-factor authentication, the recovery key and personal settings

sharedFolders.title: Shared folders and file services
sharedFolders.description: Shared folders with their rights, and the settings of SMB, SFTP, WebDAV and FTP

storage.title: Storage settings
storage.description: Restore points of the shared folders, scrub and self-test schedules

system.title: System settings
system.description: System language, formats, time zone, time servers and log retention

certificates.title: Certificates and keys
certificates.description: The certificate of this box and its SSH host keys, so clients keep trusting it

apps.title: Apps
apps.description: Installed apps with their permissions, who may use them and the app pool; the apps' files and data stay on the pool

reverseProxy.title: Reverse proxy
reverseProxy.description: Proxy hosts, redirect hosts, streams and what unknown names get; uploaded certificates come with the certificates

updates.intro: Pithyx checks once a day whether a newer version is available and tells you; it never installs by itself. Before every update the box takes a snapshot of the system and checks the new version after the restart. If that check fails, it goes back to the snapshot by itself.
updates.unsupported: Updates apply only to a box installed with the Pithyx installer. This machine is laid out differently ({reason}), so you can check for updates but not install them or roll back here.
updates.needsMinimum: This version needs at least Pithyx {minimum}. Install a version in between from an update file first.
updates.debian: {count, plural, =0 {No Debian updates.} one {# Debian update} other {# Debian updates}}{count, plural, =0 {} other {, {security, plural, =0 {none of them a security fix} one {# of them a security fix} other {# of them security fixes}}.}}

progress.title: Update in progress
progress.running: Working. Do not switch the box off.
progress.restarting: The box restarts now and checks the new version. This page reconnects by itself; the history then shows the result.

upload.title: Install from a file
upload.intro: Upload a .pithyxupdate file, for example on a box without internet. The box checks its signature and every package before anything changes.
upload.signed: Signed by a key this box trusts.
upload.unsigned: Not signed: a development file, accepted only on a development machine.
upload.details: Channel {channel}, {packages, plural, one {# package} other {# packages}}, kernel {kernel}.

snapshots.title: Snapshots
snapshots.intro: A snapshot of the system is taken before every update; the last three are kept. Going back restores the system and its settings as they were then. Pools and their files are not touched.

history.title: History
history.update: Update {from} → {to} ({source, select, online {online} file {from a file} recovery {recovery menu} other {{source}}})
history.rollback: Back from {from} to {to} ({source, select, manual {Settings} recovery {recovery menu} other {{source}}})

settings.title: Settings
settings.checkHint: The check only reads a small file from the update source and notifies administrators. Nothing installs by itself.
settings.channelHint: Stable gets releases only. Beta gets new versions earlier, for testing; a beta box also installs stable versions.

installDialog.title: Install Pithyx {version}?
installDialog.snapshot: First the box takes a snapshot of the system, so you can always go back to the current version.
installDialog.restart: Then it installs the update and restarts. Afterwards it checks the new version for up to five minutes and goes back to the snapshot by itself if the check fails. The box is not reachable during the restart.
installDialog.debian: Also install {count, plural, one {the Debian update} other {the # Debian updates}}

rollbackDialog.title: Go back to Pithyx {version}?
rollbackDialog.what: The system goes back to the snapshot of Pithyx {version} from {date} and restarts.
rollbackDialog.lost: Settings changed since then are lost (users, shared folders, apps settings). Pools and their files stay as they are.

source.title: Update source
source.name: Source
source.other: This box follows {name}, not the Pithyx project. It was switched in the recovery menu and trusts only the keys below. To go back, choose "Back to the Pithyx project" there.
source.intro: Only the recovery menu at the console switches the update source, for example to a fork, so a taken-over account cannot redirect the updates. To switch, save the source’s pithyx-source.json here (useful when you reach the console only through remote management), or put it on a USB stick, or type it in the menu.
source.choose: Save source file for the recovery menu
source.saved: {name} is saved for the recovery menu
source.savedBy: Saved by {user} on {date}. Nothing changes until it is chosen at the console.
source.next: To switch: restart the box, choose "Pithyx recovery" in the boot menu (key r), then "Change the update source" and "Use the file saved in Settings", and type the source’s name.

homes.intro: Every user has a home folder of their own. They see it as home in Files, over SMB, SFTP, WebDAV and FTP; administrators also see every home below homes. Only the user and administrators can open a home.
homes.empty: There are no home folders yet. They appear once a pool has the Pithyx layout.
homes.caption: Home folders

pool.title: Pool
pool.none: No pool can take home folders yet. The first pool with the Pithyx layout becomes the home pool.
pool.explain: New users get their home folder here. Moving copies every home folder with its files, owners and rights to the other pool.
pool.moving: The home folders are moving to another pool. The job shows how far it is.

move.title: Move the home folders to {pool}?
move.oneByOne: The home folders move one after the other, each with its files, owners, rights and recycle bin.
move.readOnly: While a home folder is copied, it can be read but not changed.
move.kept: Once a home folder arrived, it is used from the new pool and the old copy is deleted.
move.failure: If a home folder cannot be moved, it stays where it was and can be changed again; the ones moved before stay moved.

quota.title: Quota
quota.defaultHint: For every home folder without its own quota. Leave empty for no limit.
quota.invalid: Enter a number, for example 50 or 1.5.

release.label: Move the files of {folder} into a shared folder
release.title: Move the files of {folder}?
release.explain: A new folder in the shared folder gets every file of {folder}. Then the home folder is deleted with its recycle bin.
release.noShares: There is no shared folder to move the files into.

delete.label: Delete {folder}
delete.title: Delete {folder}?
delete.explain: The home folder goes with every file, its recycle bin and its snapshots. This cannot be undone. If it belongs to a user whose pool is gone, the user gets a new, empty home folder.

ups.intro: With a UPS, the box shuts down cleanly on a power failure before the battery runs out: apps and file services stop and the pools are unmounted. Pithyx reads the UPS through NUT (Network UPS Tools).

problem.refused: No NUT server answers at this address and port.
problem.timeout: The NUT server does not answer in time.
problem.unknown_ups: The NUT server has no UPS of this name.
problem.driver_not_connected: No UPS was found. Check the USB cable, or whether the NUT server sees its UPS.
problem.access_denied: The NUT server refused the user or the password.
problem.protocol: The NUT server answered with an error.

shutdown.forced: The box shuts down: the UPS's NUT server shuts every system down.
shutdown.low_battery: The box shuts down: the UPS says its battery is low.
shutdown.charge: The box shuts down: the battery reached the charge limit.
shutdown.runtime: The box shuts down: the battery reached the runtime limit.
shutdown.lost: The box shuts down: the UPS ran on battery and stopped answering.

modeHint.off: The box does not watch a UPS.
modeHint.usb: Connect the UPS with its USB cable. The box finds it by itself, and after a shutdown the UPS cuts its power, so the box starts again once the power is back (if its firmware is set to start on power).
modeHint.network: Another machine (a NAS, a router or a server with NUT) has the UPS. The box signs in as a secondary, so that machine waits for the box before it cuts the power.

ups.hostHint: Host name or address of the machine with the UPS.
ups.name: UPS name
ups.nameHint: The UPS's name on that server, as in its ups.conf.
ups.usernameHint: A user of that server's upsd.users with "upsmon secondary"; empty reads the UPS without signing in.
ups.passwordKept: A password is saved; leave the field empty to keep it.
ups.limits: On battery the box shuts down once one of these limits is reached, or when the UPS says its battery is low.
